# Tallinn Notes

## Overview

Two days in Tallinn in May, crossing from Helsinki on the two hour ferry at about 15 EUR each way. I booked the morning sailing and was in the old town by lunchtime, which made the day feel longer than the crossing suggested. The walled centre is small enough to walk end to end in half an hour, and I spent most of my time inside that ring. The weather was bright and cold, the sea wind cutting across the square even when the sun was out.

I stayed in a small guesthouse inside the walls, 60 EUR a night, with a courtyard and a cat. The trams and buses run on a card that I loaded at the port, and I used it twice, mostly walking. The city felt quiet for a capital, and the tourist crowds thinned after the day-trippers caught their evening ferry back. I gave the first day to the walls and the second to the districts outside the centre. The ferry terminal is a short walk from the old town and I did not need a taxi. The town is small enough that a map lasted me the whole two days, and I only used the card twice, both times for the tram to the outer districts.

## Food

The food is northern and heavy, built for the cold, and I ate well for modest money. The old town is full of places priced for visitors, so I ate one street back from the main square and paid about half as much for the same dishes. A plate of black bread, herring and potatoes came to 12 EUR, and a bowl of the thick barley soup with smoked pork was 7 EUR and filled me for an afternoon.

The market hall near the edge of the old town is the place for a cheap lunch, and I bought smoked fish, rye bread and a pastry for 8 EUR. Elk sausage and juniper berries turned up on several menus, and a plate with mashed potato cost 15 EUR at a plain café in the district of Telliskivi. That district is a former railway works turned into studios, bars and food trucks, and I ate dinner there twice, once from a truck for 9 EUR and once at a sit-down place for 22 EUR. The local beer is good and cheap, a half litre for 5 EUR. I finished one evening with a marzipan sweet from a café on the square, 4 EUR, and it was the best thing I ate there. The breakfast at the guesthouse was included: rye bread, cheese, cold cuts and coffee, and it held me to lunch. I bought a jar of honey and a bag of rye crackers at the market to take home, and both survived the ferry.

## Notes

The old town walls and towers are the reason to come, and a walk along the ramparts plus a climb up one of the towers cost a few euros and gave the best view of the red roofs. The viewing platforms on the hill above the centre are free and busier, and I went at dusk when the town lit up below. A day trip to Kadriorg took twenty minutes by tram and cost about 2 EUR, and the palace park and the art museum filled a quiet afternoon; the museum entry was 12 EUR. The square in the centre has a Christmas market area in winter and a market of stalls in summer, and I bought a woollen hat there when the wind won. The day trip was the best value of the two days and I would give it more time next visit. Photography from the platforms is best at sunset, and I went up twice, once in the afternoon and once at dusk, and the second was far better. The old town is compact, so the walls, the square and the viewing spots all sit within a ten-minute walk of each other. On the last morning I crossed back on the early ferry and was in Helsinki by eleven.
